title: Active Recall
desc: Retrieve information without looking at your notes.
routine: Study → Hide → Retrieve → Check → Review Later.
summary: Make a question, close your notes, answer from memory, then check. Correct gaps and return to the question later.

pages.title: Familiar is not the same as remembered
pages.body:
You reread your programming notes and every word looks familiar. In a closed-book quiz, you cannot define a queue. Recognising a definition on a page is different from producing it from memory.

Rereading can help you understand material initially, but it does not show whether you can retrieve it independently. A small retrieval attempt makes the gaps visible.

Think of a CS term you saw this week. Could you explain it with your notes closed?

pages.title: Give your memory a chance to answer
pages.body:
Active recall means bringing information to mind without looking at the answer. Retrieval is the practice, and checking is how you correct it.


• Study: understand one concept.
• Hide: close the source.
• Retrieve: answer a clear question.
• Check: compare with your notes and fix gaps.
• Review later: retrieve again after a delay.

Use it for definitions, flashcards, tracing code, or explaining why an algorithm works. A flashcard only becomes recall practice when you try before flipping.

pages.title: Watch a retrieval attempt
pages.body:
Study this definition: A stack removes the last item added first (LIFO). Imagine adding A, then B, then C.

Add AAdd BAdd C

Now hide the definition. Which item would be removed first, and why?



Check the ordering rule, not just the familiar word. If you confused stack and queue, compare LIFO and FIFO, then try again later.

pages.title: Bring it into your next study session
pages.body:
Turn a lecture heading into a question: “What does a function do?” Close your notes, explain it, then compare.


• Keep one idea per flashcard.
• Say or type an answer before revealing it.
• Record what was missing, then retrieve again later.
• Mix easy and difficult questions instead of rereading only familiar pages.

Study → Hide → Retrieve → Check → Review Later.

Your two challenges are Word Flash and Flip & Recall. Each completed challenge constructs one purple building.

title: Chunking
desc: Organise complex information into meaningful groups.
routine: Find a pattern → Group → Name → Retrieve.
summary: Group by a meaningful shared property, name each group, then reconstruct the groups without looking. Check each item belongs.

pages.title: A long list can hide a simple pattern
pages.body:
Stack, Boolean, If, Queue, String, For, Array, While, Integer. Nine separate terms can feel like nine unrelated things to hold in mind.

But they share meaningful properties. Finding those properties gives you a small number of group labels to use as retrieval cues.

Which of these terms describe collections? Which describe decisions or repetition?

pages.title: Group by meaning
pages.body:
Chunking organises separate pieces into meaningful groups. A familiar group can be treated as one organised unit rather than many unrelated items.


• Look for a shared function, category, or pattern.
• Group items that genuinely belong together.
• Give each group a useful name.
• Hide the list and reconstruct each group.

Use categories for revision, logical stages for procedures, and patterns for code. Chunking supports organisation; you still need to understand and retrieve the items.

pages.title: From scattered terms to three chunks
pages.body:
Before: Stack · Boolean · If · Queue · String · For · Array · While · Integer.

Data Structures

Stack · Queue · Array

Control Flow

Data Types

Integer · Boolean · String

“Data Structures” cues a group; the ordering rule still distinguishes stack from queue. Grouping by first letter alone would not explain their roles.

pages.title: Organise, then retrieve
pages.body:
For your next lecture, put concepts into categories such as “stores data”, “controls execution”, and “describes a value”. Then close the page and recreate the groups.


• Use a label that explains the relationship.
• Keep groups small enough to understand.
• Split groups that mix unrelated roles.
• Check the individual details after retrieving a group.

A neat-looking group can still be misleading. Check that each item belongs for the reason you chose.

Practise with Sort & Remember and Code Breaker to build your blue district.

title: Association and Elaboration
desc: Connect new concepts with familiar ideas.
routine: Connect → Explain the link → Check its limits → Retrieve.
summary: Create a familiar image or story and explain exactly how it connects. State where the analogy stops matching the technical concept.

pages.title: New words need somewhere to connect
pages.body:
“Stack” and “Queue” may look like two arbitrary labels. Yet you already know how plates are stacked and how people wait in a line.

A familiar experience can become a cue for a new technical idea. Explaining the connection helps you remember why it fits.

blocks.text: “Stack” and “Queue” may look like two arbitrary labels. Yet you already know how plates are stacked and how people wait in a line.

pages.title: Build a link and explain it
pages.body:
Association links a new idea with something familiar. Elaboration adds meaning by explaining how and why the connection works.


• Choose a familiar image, example, or story.
• Connect a specific feature to the new concept.
• Explain the connection in your own words.
• Check the technical definition and the analogy’s limits.

A strange story may be memorable, but it must still cue the right concepts. “They are both things” is a weak link because it explains little.

pages.title: A queue is like a waiting line
pages.body:
Queue → people waiting in lineThe person who arrives first is served first. A queue removes the earliest item added first: FIFO.



A stack of plates instead cues LIFO. A labelled container cues a variable, and repeated laps cue a loop.

Where the analogy stops: people may jump a real-world line; a standard queue follows its defined operations. Variables obey language rules, and loops need a condition or count.

pages.title: Make connections that carry meaning
pages.body:
• Choose a familiar example with a precise shared feature.
• Say why the connection works.
• State what the analogy does not capture.
• Hide the analogy and retrieve the technical concept.

Example story: “A labelled variable stores a ticket number. A function checks it, a loop repeats the checks, and a queue serves people in arrival order.”

title: Spaced Repetition
desc: Return to ideas across time to make them last.
routine: Retrieve today → Review later → Adjust the interval.
summary: Use questions across several days. Review missed items sooner; extend the interval after successful recall. Keep sessions manageable.

pages.title: Forgetting gives you useful information
pages.body:
You could define a function yesterday, but today the definition is hazy. This is normal: a successful answer immediately after study is different from recall after a delay.

Instead of cramming every review into one sitting, return to questions across time. A difficult retrieval tells you what needs attention.

pages.title: Space your retrieval attempts
pages.body:
Spaced repetition combines retrieval with review sessions separated in time. It gives you opportunities to retrieve after some forgetting.


• Learn and retrieve a concept today.
• Schedule a later review.
• Check your answer before rating it.
• Review missed concepts sooner.
• Gradually extend intervals after successful recall.

Keep sessions short. Prioritise what is due and what you missed, rather than only what feels easy.

pages.title: One possible review schedule
pages.body:
Day 1 → Day 2 → Day 4 → Day 7

1234567891011121314

Retrieve on each highlighted day. If you miss “Queue” on Day 2, check FIFO and review it sooner. If you recall “Function” reliably, leave a longer gap.

These are illustrative intervals, not universal rules. Adjust them to difficulty, your timetable, and when you need the knowledge.

pages.title: A realistic review habit
pages.body:
• Use questions you can answer without notes.
• Schedule review in advance.
• Bring missed concepts back sooner.
• Track dates as well as scores.
• Do not treat immediate replay as delayed retention.

Memory Comeback uses your earlier mistakes, with labelled example history available for testing. Rescue Forgotten Words gives missed items another chance.

Your city stays built if you miss a day. Come back when you can and continue.

title: Explain and Apply
desc: Explain simply. Put your understanding to work.
routine: Explain → Find gaps → Check → Apply → Refine.
summary: Explain without notes, compare with an accurate source, fix gaps, and solve a fresh example. Simplicity should preserve the key technical details.

pages.title: Can you explain it without the slide?
pages.body:
You recognise “Function” on a slide, but explaining it to a classmate reveals a gap: why would you use one?

Explaining makes missing details visible. Applying the idea to a new situation checks whether you can use it beyond the original example.

pages.title: Explain, check, and transfer
pages.body:
• Close your notes and explain the idea simply.
• Include the defining details, not just an analogy.
• Notice where you hesitate or become vague.
• Check a reliable source and correct gaps.
• Apply the idea to an unfamiliar situation.

Simple language should stay technically accurate. “A function does stuff” is short but misses that it is a reusable block for a specific task.

pages.title: From explanation to a decision
pages.body:
Explain: A stack removes the most recently added item first (LIFO). A queue removes the earliest added item first (FIFO).

Apply: A text editor must undo the latest action first. Choose a stack because the required removal order is LIFO.

A printer serving jobs in arrival order needs a queue. The choice follows the ordering requirement, rather than which word feels familiar.

pages.title: Turn recall into usable understanding
pages.body:
• Explain without looking first.
• Include what distinguishes the concept.
• Check missing details and correct errors.
• Solve a new scenario and explain the choice.
• Retrieve the refined explanation later.

Teach the Robot provides transparent checklist feedback. Knowledge Detective asks you to choose concepts for practical situations.

Scores show performance on these activities. They do not establish improvement in general memory ability.
